title: Machine Learning with Python
summary: Regression, classification, clustering and model selection with scikit-learn.
concepts: Regression: predict a continuous target; classification: predict a class or its probability. Choose metrics that match the decision.
A pipeline fits preprocessing on each training fold. Fit scalers and imputers after splitting to avoid leakage.
Cross-validation selects hyperparameters on the training partition. The final test partition stays untouched until the model choice is fixed.
For clustering, inspect stability and domain meaning as well as silhouette scores. PCA summarizes variance; t-SNE and UMAP are primarily exploratory views.
formula: Precision = TP / (TP + FP); recall = TP / (TP + FN); F1 = 2PR / (P + R). MAE and RMSE use target units; R² compares squared error to a mean predictor.
revisit: Compare a DummyClassifier with a scaled logistic-regression pipeline using the same folds.
Revisit the rainfall project; record class balance, preprocessing, split rule and confusion matrix.
Explain when a stratified random split would be inappropriate, such as grouped customers or time series.
pitfalls: Preprocessing all data before splitting leaks information.
Training accuracy and a single favorable split can hide weak generalization.
Several exercise cells contain deliberate syntax blanks; inspect the catalog before using Run All.
questions: Why does scaling belong inside the pipeline?
Which error is more costly in a chosen application: false positives or false negatives?
When would PR-AUC be more useful than accuracy?

title: Introduction to Deep Learning and Neural Networks with Keras
summary: Forward propagation, backpropagation, activation functions and first Keras models.
concepts: A dense layer computes an affine transformation followed by an activation. Nonlinear activations allow a network to learn nonlinear relationships.
Backpropagation applies the chain rule to compute gradients. The optimizer updates parameters; it does not define the loss.
Choose the output layer and loss together: logits and cross-entropy for classification, a continuous output and a regression loss for regression.
Validation curves guide regularization and stopping. A final test set is for evaluation after architecture decisions.
formula: For a batch X of shape (B, d), a dense layer with h units maps XW + b to shape (B, h). Gradient descent updates θ ← θ − η∇θL.
revisit: Trace the shapes through a two-layer dense model before running it.
Compare a linear baseline with a small MLP while fixing the split and training budget.
Inspect the aircraft damage classification and captioning starter; distinguish discriminative and generative outputs.
pitfalls: Large networks can memorize small datasets.
Softmax probabilities and raw logits require matching loss settings.
The final project has unfinished hyperparameter assignments; it is a study template.
questions: What does a vanishing gradient do to early layers?
How do batch size and learning rate affect optimization?
Why does low training loss fail to prove useful generalization?

title: Deep Learning with Keras and TensorFlow
summary: Functional models, transfer learning, generative models and reinforcement-learning introductions.
concepts: Use the Functional API for models with multiple branches or shared layers. A custom Layer owns reusable computation and trainable state.
Transfer learning starts from a pretrained representation. Freeze the backbone first, then consider a smaller learning rate for fine-tuning.
Autoencoders reconstruct inputs; GANs learn through a generator-discriminator objective; diffusion models learn a denoising process.
Q-learning estimates action values. A DQN replaces the value table with a neural network and needs a carefully controlled training loop.
formula: A custom training step computes predictions, evaluates the loss under GradientTape, differentiates with respect to trainable variables, and applies optimizer gradients.
revisit: Sketch the data flow for the Functional API notebook, including each tensor shape.
Compare a frozen feature extractor with fine-tuning using identical validation data.
Use the waste classification starter to record augmentation, split rules and class-level errors.
pitfalls: Augmentation belongs on training data; validation should reflect the intended evaluation distribution.
Unfreezing layers without reviewing normalization behavior and learning rates can damage pretrained representations.

questions: When does subclassing help more than a Sequential model?
How would you isolate the effect of data augmentation?

title: Introduction to Neural Networks and PyTorch
summary: Tensors, autograd, datasets and gradient-based learning.
concepts: A tensor has a shape, dtype and device. Check all three at the boundaries of a model.
Autograd records differentiable operations. backward() accumulates gradients, so clear them between optimization steps.
Dataset describes samples; DataLoader groups and optionally shuffles them. Shuffle training examples without mixing the evaluation partition into training.
For binary logits use BCEWithLogitsLoss; for multiclass logits use CrossEntropyLoss with integer class indices.
formula: The training loop is zero_grad → forward → loss → backward → step. Evaluation uses model.eval() together with a no-gradient context.
revisit: Run the companion PyTorch training loop and inspect the train/validation/test separation.
Compare full-batch, stochastic and mini-batch gradient descent on the same regression problem.
Review the match predictor starter and write down features that would leak the final match result.
pitfalls: eval() changes layer behavior; it does not disable gradient recording.
The source named Wine Classification actually loads the breast-cancer dataset; the curated title follows the content.

questions: Why do gradients accumulate by default?

title: Deep Learning with PyTorch
summary: Multilayer networks, initialization, optimization, normalization, CNNs and transfer learning.
concepts: Hidden layers build representations; nonlinearities control which functions a network can express.
Initialization and normalization influence activation and gradient scales. Compare them under the same seed, data and training budget.
Convolution shares local filters. Pooling and strided convolutions change spatial resolution and affect the receptive field.
Dropout and batch normalization behave differently during training and evaluation. Save the chosen model state and evaluate with the correct mode.
formula: A 2D convolution output size per spatial axis is floor((input + 2·padding − dilation·(kernel − 1) − 1) / stride + 1).
revisit: Calculate CNN tensor shapes before executing the MNIST notebook.
Compare initialization choices with a fixed optimizer and plot both training and validation loss.
Use the collected Fashion-MNIST project as a separate classification study; document the label mapping and split.
pitfalls: Flattening the wrong dimensions mixes examples or changes the classifier input size.
Selecting the best epoch on the test set contaminates the final estimate.
A saved checkpoint is useful only if it can be reloaded into the matching architecture.
questions: How does a convolution reduce the number of learned parameters?
When can dropout hurt a small model?
How would you compare two initializations fairly?

title: AI Capstone Project with Deep Learning
summary: Satellite land classification with Keras, PyTorch, vision transformers and CNN–ViT integration.
concepts: Build a dataset inventory before training: class counts, image dimensions, duplicate images and split membership.
Keep data preprocessing and class mappings consistent when comparing Keras and PyTorch classifiers.
A vision transformer converts image patches into token embeddings and models their relationships with attention.
A hybrid CNN–ViT combines local visual features with attention. Compare it to simpler baselines under an explicit resource budget.
formula: For square images of side H and patch size P, the image contributes (H/P)² patch tokens when H is divisible by P. Attention cost grows with the square of the token count.
revisit: Start with data loading, then preprocessing and augmentation, then the framework-specific classifiers.

title: Generative AI and LLMs: Architecture and Data Preparation
summary: Tokenization, vocabulary design and data loaders for language models.
concepts: A tokenizer maps text into model-specific token IDs. The tokenizer, vocabulary and model checkpoint must agree.
Padding tokens align sequence lengths; an attention mask distinguishes real input from padding.
A causal language model predicts the next token. Shift inputs and targets consistently.
Data splitting must prevent duplicated or overlapping documents from contaminating evaluation.
formula: Typical token IDs and attention masks have shape (batch, sequence_length); embeddings have shape (batch, sequence_length, hidden_size).
revisit: Inspect the tokenization of punctuation, accented text and an unfamiliar word.
Build a tiny padded batch and verify the mask by hand.
Trace the text-to-batch transformations in the NLP data loader.
pitfalls: Token count differs from word count and affects context limits and cost.
Legacy torchtext imports have strict binary compatibility requirements.
Some source install cells request newer torch with old torchtext; those combinations are not a validated environment.
questions: Why must inference use the training tokenizer?
How should padding be excluded from loss computation?

title: Gen AI Foundational Models for NLP and Language Understanding
summary: N-gram models, word embeddings, feedforward language models and sequence-to-sequence models.
concepts: An n-gram model estimates the next token from a fixed context. Smoothing helps when a context is unseen.
Word embeddings learn continuous representations; similarity reflects the training objective and corpus.
Sequence models track order. A sequence-to-sequence model maps an input sequence to an output sequence of potentially different length.
Document classification aggregates token-level information into a prediction; padding and pooling choices affect the representation.
formula: A causal sequence likelihood factors as P(x₁…xₜ) = ∏ P(xᵢ | x₁…xᵢ₋₁). Perplexity is exp(mean token negative log-likelihood).
revisit: Compare unigram and bigram predictions on a tiny corpus with unseen contexts.
Explore nearest neighbors for Word2Vec embeddings and identify corpus bias.
Trace teacher forcing through the translation notebook.
pitfalls: A low training perplexity can reflect memorization.
Averaging embeddings discards order and can confuse negation.
Evaluate translation on held-out sequences rather than cherry-picked generated examples.
questions: What information does bag-of-words discard?
Why is teacher forcing different from inference?
When can embedding similarity be misleading?

title: Generative AI Language Modeling with Transformers
summary: Self-attention, positional encoding, BERT-style encoders and causal decoders.
concepts: Attention mixes value vectors according to query-key similarity. Multiple heads learn different projections.
Position information is needed because self-attention alone does not encode sequence order.
Encoder models support bidirectional context; a causal decoder masks future tokens. Their training objectives differ.
Attention masks, padding masks and label shifts have distinct roles. Inspect them with a short synthetic sequence.
formula: Attention(Q,K,V) = softmax(QKᵀ / √dₖ + mask)V. A causal mask excludes keys at positions later than the query position.
revisit: Compute a small attention matrix by hand and confirm each row sums to one.
Compare a BERT masked-token target with a decoder next-token target.
Review the classifier and translation notebooks, identifying the task-specific output heads.
pitfalls: Mask shape errors can silently allow future-token leakage.
Applying softmax over the wrong axis changes the computation.
Several collected transformer exercise cells are intentionally incomplete; the audit lists their locations.
questions: Why scale attention scores by √dₖ?
What changes when a decoder sees future tokens during training?
How does sequence length affect attention memory?

title: Generative AI Engineering and Fine-Tuning Transformers
summary: Inference, pretraining, task adaptation, adapters and LoRA.
concepts: Pretraining learns general representations; fine-tuning adapts parameters to a task or domain. Evaluate both on the same held-out examples.
Adapters add trainable modules while most base weights stay frozen. LoRA learns a low-rank update to selected weight matrices.
Parameter efficiency reduces trainable state but does not eliminate base-model memory or activation cost.
A reproducible adapter result requires the base revision, tokenizer, adapter checkpoint, generation settings and an exact reload test.
formula: LoRA represents ΔW = (α/r)BA, where B has shape (out_features,r) and A has shape (r,in_features). Its trainable parameter count is r·(in_features + out_features).
revisit: Count trainable versus total parameters in the adapter and LoRA labs.
Compare the base model and adapter with identical prompts and decoding settings.
Reload the saved adapter in a fresh process before describing it as a reusable artifact.
pitfalls: Lower training loss alone does not prove a better downstream model.
The collected Hugging Face inference notebook had 10 saved error outputs; they were cleared and recorded in provenance.
Quantization, padding and tokenizer changes can confound base-versus-adapter comparisons.
questions: Which memory costs remain when base weights are frozen?
What makes an adapter evaluation a fair comparison?
Why does checkpoint reload matter separately from training success?

title: Generative AI Advanced Fine-Tuning for LLMs
summary: Instruction tuning, reward models, PPO and direct preference optimization.
concepts: Instruction tuning learns from prompt-response examples. Template consistency and label masking are part of the training specification.
A reward model estimates preference from comparison data; its score is a learned proxy with its own biases.
PPO optimizes a policy using a reward signal and a constraint against drifting too far from a reference policy.
DPO uses chosen/rejected response pairs directly. Data quality and reference-model assumptions affect its behavior.
formula: A preference record contains a prompt, a chosen response and a rejected response. Keep related prompts together when forming train/evaluation partitions.
revisit: Inspect chosen/rejected pairs for labeling errors and near duplicates.
Explain the role of the reference model before running PPO or DPO.
Design a held-out preference evaluation including regressions on factual and refusal behavior.
pitfalls: Optimizing a reward score can exploit weaknesses in the reward model.
Preference wins do not establish factual accuracy or domain safety.
TRL APIs vary by version; the course pins are reference snapshots, not a tested unified environment.
questions: What can a reward model get wrong?
How does DPO use the rejected response?

title: Fundamentals of AI Agents Using RAG and LangChain
summary: Prompt templates, retrieval-augmented generation, document summarization and tool use.
concepts: A retriever selects evidence; a generator writes an answer conditioned on that evidence. Evaluate those stages separately.
Chunk boundaries, overlap and metadata determine what can be retrieved and cited. Preserve stable source IDs.
An agent selects actions or tools. Tool calls need explicit inputs, observable results and bounded execution.
Prompt text from a retrieved document is untrusted data; it should not redefine application instructions.
formula: Recall@k is the fraction of relevant items found among the top k results. For queries with one expected source, Hit@k checks whether that source appears in the top k.
revisit: Run the local retrieval companion to inspect ranking, source attribution and an unsupported query.
Trace a document through loading, chunking, indexing, retrieval and answer construction.
Review the weather-agent starter and identify required credentials and external requests before execution.
pitfalls: A fluent answer does not prove that the retrieved evidence supports it.
Retrieval scores are ranking signals rather than calibrated confidence probabilities.
Cloud-backed labs depend on provider credentials and current APIs; no live calls were made during curation.
questions: How do you tell a retrieval failure from a generation failure?

title: Project: Generative AI Applications with RAG and LangChain
summary: Document loaders, splitting, embeddings, vector stores, retrievers and a Gradio QA interface.
concepts: Keep ingestion separate from answering so documents are not repeatedly parsed and embedded for every query.
Choose chunk size and overlap using retrieval evidence, not the maximum model context alone.
Persist source identifiers alongside embeddings, then return source references with answers.
A usable QA app needs failure handling for empty files, unsupported questions, provider errors and private data.
formula: The application flow is document → loader → chunks → embeddings → index → retriever → prompt context → model response → source references.
